concepts.title: Galvanic and Electrolytic Cells
concepts.definition: Two mirror-image devices built from electrodes in electrolytes: a galvanic cell turns the energy of a spontaneous redox change into electricity, while an electrolytic cell spends electricity to force a non-spontaneous one.
concepts.formula: cell type = function of external voltage versus cell emf
concepts.key_idea: Oxidation always sits at the anode and reduction at the cathode; in a galvanic cell the anode is negative, the current convention runs opposite to electron flow, and a salt bridge joins the two half-cells.
question_patterns: differentiate a galvanic cell from an electrolytic cell in terms of energy change and spontaneity
identify which electrode is the anode and which is the cathode in the Daniell cell
state what happens in a galvanic cell when the opposing external voltage crosses the cell emf
explain the role of the salt bridge in a cell drawn as metal and electrolyte pairs
predict the direction of electron flow and of conventional current in a working voltaic cell
write the cell notation for the zinc and copper couple with the anode on the left

solution_steps.action: Split the overall reaction into oxidation and reduction halves
solution_steps.explain: For the Daniell cell, zinc loses electrons at the anode and copper ions gain them at the cathode.

solution_steps.action: Label the half-cells and their signs
solution_steps.explain: Oxidation half-cell is the anode (negative in a galvanic cell); reduction half-cell is the cathode (positive).

solution_steps.action: Compare the applied external voltage with the cell emf
solution_steps.explain: Below the emf the cell runs as galvanic, at the emf nothing flows, above it the same setup works as an electrolytic cell in reverse.

concepts.title: Standard Cell Potential from Electrode Potentials
concepts.definition: The emf of a cell comes from subtracting the standard reduction potential of the left (anode) half-cell from that of the right (cathode) half-cell, each read from the tabulated electrode potential series.
concepts.key_idea: A positive result confirms the reaction runs as written; the more negative electrode supplies the reducing agent, and individual half-cell potentials are always measured against the hydrogen electrode set at zero.
concepts.textbook_ref: lech102.txt, Section 2.2 and Table 2.1 (Standard Electrode Potentials)
question_patterns: calculate the standard emf of the Daniell cell from the zinc and copper electrode potentials
find e0 cell for the reaction of chromium metal with cadmium ions using standard reduction potentials
determine the standard cell potential of the iron and silver couple
what emf follows when the cathode potential is 0.34 V and the anode potential is minus 0.76 V
compute the standard potential of a galvanic cell assembled from two listed half-cells
work out e0 for the cell representation with the anode written on the left

solution_steps.action: Read the standard reduction potentials from the series
solution_steps.explain: Copper sits at plus 0.34 V and zinc at minus 0.76 V in the standard table.

solution_steps.action: Subtract the left electrode value from the right electrode value
solution_steps.explain: 0.34 minus minus 0.76 gives 1.10 V for the Daniell cell; a positive value means the cell reaction is spontaneous as written.

worked_examples.question: Using Standard Cell Potential from Electrode Potentials, compute the result for e0_cathode = 3, e0_anode = 3.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Read the standard reduction potentials from the series: e0_pair = e0_cathode - e0_anode = 0.0 Step 2: Subtract the left electrode value from the right electrode value: e0_cell = e0_pair * 1.0 = 0.0 Final result: 0.0

worked_examples.question: Using Standard Cell Potential from Electrode Potentials, compute the result for e0_cathode = 4, e0_anode = 4.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Read the standard reduction potentials from the series: e0_pair = e0_cathode - e0_anode = 0.0 Step 2: Subtract the left electrode value from the right electrode value: e0_cell = e0_pair * 1.0 = 0.0 Final result: 0.0

concepts.title: Nernst Equation for Cell emf at 298 K
concepts.definition: Non-standard concentrations pull the cell voltage away from its standard value by an amount governed by the reaction quotient: the emf drops as products pile up relative to reactants.
concepts.key_idea: Build the reaction quotient from the given ion concentrations, take its base-10 logarithm, then correct the standard emf with 0.059 divided by the electron count per formula unit of the reaction.
question_patterns: calculate the emf of the cell in which magnesium reacts with 0.0001 M silver ions using the Nernst equation
find the cell potential at 298 K for the nickel and silver couple with stated ion concentrations
determine e cell for a Daniell cell when the zinc ion and copper ion concentrations are not unity
apply the Nernst relation to get the voltage of a galvanic cell from its standard emf and the reaction quotient
what is the electrode potential of hydrogen in contact with a solution of pH 10
use the Nernst equation to correct a standard emf for the given product and reactant concentrations

solution_steps.action: Form the reaction quotient from the stated concentrations
solution_steps.explain: For the magnesium and silver cell, Q = 0.130 times 0.0001 squared, whose base-10 logarithm is about minus 7.11.

solution_steps.action: Correct the standard emf with the Nernst term
solution_steps.explain: 3.17 minus 0.059 over 2, all times minus 7.11, leaves about 2.96 V for the cell.

worked_examples.question: Using Nernst Equation for Cell emf at 298 K, compute the result for log10_of_q = 3, e0_cell = 3, n_electrons = 3.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Form the reaction quotient from the stated concentrations: log_quotient = log10_of_q * 1.0 = 3.0 Step 2: Correct the standard emf with the Nernst term: e_cell = e0_cell - (0.059 / n_electrons) * log_quotient = 2.941 Final result: 2.941

worked_examples.question: Using Nernst Equation for Cell emf at 298 K, compute the result for log10_of_q = 4, e0_cell = 4, n_electrons = 4.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Form the reaction quotient from the stated concentrations: log_quotient = log10_of_q * 1.0 = 4.0 Step 2: Correct the standard emf with the Nernst term: e_cell = e0_cell - (0.059 / n_electrons) * log_quotient = 3.941 Final result: 3.941

concepts.title: Equilibrium Constant from Standard Cell Potential
concepts.definition: At equilibrium the cell voltage falls to zero, so the standard emf alone fixes the equilibrium constant of the cell reaction through a simple logarithmic relation.
concepts.key_idea: Multiply n by the standard emf, divide by 0.059 V to get log Kc, then raise 10 to that power; equilibrium constants that are hard to measure directly come straight out of table data.
question_patterns: calculate the equilibrium constant of the copper and silver ion reaction whose standard emf is 0.46 V
find Kc for a cell reaction from its standard potential of 1.1 V and two transferred electrons
determine the equilibrium constant for the iron and silver cell at 298 K
what is Kc when the standard cell emf and the number of electrons exchanged are known
obtain the equilibrium constant of a redox reaction from tabulated electrode potentials
evaluate log Kc and then Kc for a galvanic cell with the given standard emf

solution_steps.action: Convert the standard emf into log Kc
solution_steps.explain: 2 times 0.46 over 0.059 gives about 15.6 for the copper silver cell.

solution_steps.action: Raise ten to the power of log Kc
solution_steps.explain: Ten to the 15.6 is about 3.92 times ten to the 15, an enormous constant typical of working cells.

worked_examples.question: Using Equilibrium Constant from Standard Cell Potential, compute the result for n_electrons = 0.5, e0_cell = 0.25.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Convert the standard emf into log Kc: log_kc = n_electrons * e0_cell / 0.059 = 2.118644 Step 2: Raise ten to the power of log Kc: kc = 10 ** log_kc = 131.414736 Final result: 131.414736

worked_examples.question: Using Equilibrium Constant from Standard Cell Potential, compute the result for n_electrons = 0.25, e0_cell = 0.1.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Convert the standard emf into log Kc: log_kc = n_electrons * e0_cell / 0.059 = 0.423729 Step 2: Raise ten to the power of log Kc: kc = 10 ** log_kc = 2.652948 Final result: 2.652948

concepts.title: Gibbs Energy of the Cell Reaction
concepts.definition: The electrical work a cell can deliver reversibly equals the fall in Gibbs energy, which follows from the emf multiplied by the total charge the electrons carry.
concepts.key_idea: Delta G equals minus nFE, so the sign is negative for a working cell; doubling the reaction equation doubles n and hence the Gibbs energy but leaves the emf unchanged.
question_patterns: calculate the standard Gibbs energy of the Daniell cell reaction whose emf is 1.1 V
find delta G naught for a cell with standard emf 0.36 V and two electrons transferred
determine the Gibbs energy change for the reaction in a galvanic cell at standard conditions
what is the maximum electrical work available from a cell of the given emf and electron count
compute DrGo from nF times the standard cell potential
how much Gibbs energy is released when one mole of reaction runs in the stated cell

solution_steps.action: Multiply the charge per mole of reaction by the emf and negate
solution_steps.explain: Minus 2 times 96487 coulomb per mol times 1.1 V gives minus 212270 J per mol.

solution_steps.action: Report the result in kilojoules per mole
solution_steps.explain: Divide by 1000: about minus 212.27 kJ per mol for the Daniell reaction.

worked_examples.question: Using Gibbs Energy of the Cell Reaction, compute the result for n_electrons = 3, faraday_const = 3, e0_cell = 3.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Multiply the charge per mole of reaction by the emf and negate: gibbs_j = (0 - n_electrons * faraday_const * e0_cell) = -27.0 Step 2: Report the result in kilojoules per mole: gibbs_kj = gibbs_j / 1000 = -0.027 Final result: -0.027

worked_examples.question: Using Gibbs Energy of the Cell Reaction, compute the result for n_electrons = 4, faraday_const = 4, e0_cell = 4.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Multiply the charge per mole of reaction by the emf and negate: gibbs_j = (0 - n_electrons * faraday_const * e0_cell) = -64.0 Step 2: Report the result in kilojoules per mole: gibbs_kj = gibbs_j / 1000 = -0.064 Final result: -0.064

concepts.title: Cell Constant and Conductivity from Resistance
concepts.definition: A conductivity cell is characterised by its cell constant, the electrode gap divided by electrode area; measured resistance converts to conductivity once this constant is fixed with a standard potassium chloride solution.
concepts.key_idea: Cell constant G star equals conductivity times resistance; the same product then gives any solution's conductivity as cell constant over its measured resistance.
question_patterns: calculate the conductivity of 0.02 M KCl solution if the same cell reads 100 ohm for 0.1 M KCl and 520 ohm for the unknown
find the cell constant of a conductivity cell from the resistance of a standard KCl filling
determine the conductivity of a solution whose resistance in a calibrated cell is given
what is the cell constant when the resistance is 1500 ohm and the KCl conductivity is 0.146 times ten to the minus 3 S per cm
use a standard potassium chloride solution to calibrate a conductivity cell and then read an unknown conductivity
convert a measured resistance into conductivity with the help of the cell constant

solution_steps.action: Fix the cell constant with the standard filling
solution_steps.explain: 1.29 S per m times 100 ohm gives 129 per m for the cell geometry.

solution_steps.action: Divide the cell constant by the unknown resistance
solution_steps.explain: 129 over 520 ohm leaves 0.248 S per m for the 0.02 M KCl solution.

worked_examples.question: Using Cell Constant and Conductivity from Resistance, compute the result for kappa_known = 3, resistance_known = 3, resistance_unknown = 3.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Fix the cell constant with the standard filling: cell_const = kappa_known * resistance_known = 9.0 Step 2: Divide the cell constant by the unknown resistance: kappa_unknown = cell_const / resistance_unknown = 3.0 Final result: 3.0

worked_examples.question: Using Cell Constant and Conductivity from Resistance, compute the result for kappa_known = 4, resistance_known = 4, resistance_unknown = 4.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Fix the cell constant with the standard filling: cell_const = kappa_known * resistance_known = 16.0 Step 2: Divide the cell constant by the unknown resistance: kappa_unknown = cell_const / resistance_unknown = 4.0 Final result: 4.0

concepts.title: Molar Conductivity from Conductivity
concepts.definition: The conductance of the volume of solution holding one mole of electrolyte between electrodes a unit distance apart; it scales the measured conductivity up by a thousand and divides by the molar concentration.
concepts.key_idea: Conductivity falls on dilution while molar conductivity rises, because the volume holding one mole grows; with kappa in S per cm and c in mol per litre the answer arrives in S cm2 per mol.
question_patterns: calculate the molar conductivity of 0.20 M KCl whose conductivity is 0.0248 S per cm
find lambda m for a solution from its conductivity and molar concentration
determine the molar conductivity of 0.00241 M acetic acid with conductivity 7.896 times ten to the minus 5 S per cm
what is the molar conductivity when the conductivity of the solution and its molarity are known
convert the measured conductivity of an electrolyte solution into S cm2 per mol units
compute lambda m for the given electrolyte concentration and report it in the usual units

solution_steps.action: Scale conductivity to one mole of electrolyte
solution_steps.explain: Multiply kappa by the 1000 cubic cm in a litre, then divide by molarity; 1000 times 0.0248 over 0.2 gives 124 S cm2 per mol.

worked_examples.question: Using Molar Conductivity from Conductivity, compute the result for kappa = 3, molarity = 3.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Scale conductivity to one mole of electrolyte: lambda_m = 1000 * kappa / molarity = 1000.0 Final result: 1000.0

worked_examples.question: Using Molar Conductivity from Conductivity, compute the result for kappa = 4, molarity = 4.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Scale conductivity to one mole of electrolyte: lambda_m = 1000 * kappa / molarity = 1000.0 Final result: 1000.0

concepts.title: Kohlrausch Law of Independent Migration
concepts.definition: At infinite dilution every ion drifts on its own, so an electrolyte's limiting molar conductivity is just the coefficient-weighted sum of its cation and anion contributions.
concepts.key_idea: Read limiting ionic conductivities from the table and add them with their stoichiometric factors; differences between related salts stay constant, which is how values for weak electrolytes are pieced together by combination.
question_patterns: calculate the limiting molar conductivity of CaCl2 from the limiting ionic conductivities
find lambda naught for MgSO4 using Kohlrausch law and the ion data
determine the limiting molar conductivity of acetic acid by combining the values for HCl, NaAc and NaCl
what is lambda naught m of an electrolyte expressed through its ions' individual contributions
apply the law of independent migration of ions to build the limiting molar conductivity of a salt
compute the infinite dilution molar conductivity of a weak acid from strong electrolyte data

solution_steps.action: Weight the cation contribution by its count
solution_steps.explain: For CaCl2 the calcium term is 1 times 119.0 S cm2 per mol.

solution_steps.action: Weight the anion contribution by its count
solution_steps.explain: The chloride term is 2 times 76.3, that is 152.6 S cm2 per mol.

solution_steps.action: Add the two contributions
solution_steps.explain: 119.0 plus 152.6 gives 271.6 S cm2 per mol for CaCl2; combination tricks like HCl plus NaAc minus NaCl give weak acid values the same way.

worked_examples.question: Using Kohlrausch Law of Independent Migration, compute the result for n_cation = 3, lambda_cation = 3, n_anion = 3, lambda_anion = 2.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Weight the cation contribution by its count: term_cation = n_cation * lambda_cation = 9.0 Step 2: Weight the anion contribution by its count: term_anion = n_anion * lambda_anion = 6.0 Step 3: Add the two contributions: lambda0 = term_cation + term_anion = 15.0 Final result: 15.0

worked_examples.question: Using Kohlrausch Law of Independent Migration, compute the result for n_cation = 4, lambda_cation = 4, n_anion = 4, lambda_anion = 3.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Weight the cation contribution by its count: term_cation = n_cation * lambda_cation = 16.0 Step 2: Weight the anion contribution by its count: term_anion = n_anion * lambda_anion = 12.0 Step 3: Add the two contributions: lambda0 = term_cation + term_anion = 28.0 Final result: 28.0

concepts.title: Degree of Dissociation and Ka of a Weak Electrolyte
concepts.definition: For a weak electrolyte the fraction dissociated at a given concentration equals the ratio of its molar conductivity to its limiting value, and that fraction feeds the classic Ostwald expression for the dissociation constant.
concepts.key_idea: First get lambda m from conductivity, divide by lambda naught to reach alpha, then c alpha squared over one minus alpha; weak electrolytes cannot be extrapolated, so Kohlrausch law supplies lambda naught.
concepts.textbook_ref: lech102.txt, Section 2.5 weak electrolyte discussion, equations 2.26-2.27 and Example 2.9
question_patterns: calculate the degree of dissociation and dissociation constant of 0.025 M methanoic acid given its molar conductivity
find alpha and Ka for acetic acid whose 0.001028 M solution has conductivity 4.95 times ten to the minus 5 S per cm
determine the dissociation constant of a weak acid from its molar conductivity at a stated concentration
what is the degree of dissociation when lambda m and lambda naught of a weak electrolyte are known
use the relation c alpha squared over one minus alpha to get Ka for a weak electrolyte
compute how far a dilute weak acid is ionised from conductivity data

solution_steps.action: Get the molar conductivity at the working concentration
solution_steps.explain: 1000 times 4.95e-5 over 0.001028 gives about 48.15 S cm2 per mol.

solution_steps.action: Take the ratio to the limiting molar conductivity
solution_steps.explain: 48.15 over 390.5 gives alpha near 0.123 for this acetic acid solution.

solution_steps.action: Apply the Ostwald dilution expression
solution_steps.explain: 0.001028 times alpha squared over one minus alpha gives Ka near 1.78e-5 mol per litre; the tiny floor inside the divisor only guards the arithmetic for fully dissociated edge cases.

worked_examples.question: Using Degree of Dissociation and Ka of a Weak Electrolyte, compute the result for kappa = 3, molarity = 3, lambda0 = 3.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Get the molar conductivity at the working concentration: lambda_m = 1000 * kappa / molarity = 1000.0 Step 2: Take the ratio to the limiting molar conductivity: alpha = lambda_m / lambda0 = 333.333333 Step 3: Apply the Ostwald dilution expression: ka = molarity * alpha ** 2 / max(1 - alpha, 0.001) = 333333333.333333 Final result: 333333333.333333

worked_examples.question: Using Degree of Dissociation and Ka of a Weak Electrolyte, compute the result for kappa = 4, molarity = 4, lambda0 = 4.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Get the molar conductivity at the working concentration: lambda_m = 1000 * kappa / molarity = 1000.0 Step 2: Take the ratio to the limiting molar conductivity: alpha = lambda_m / lambda0 = 250.0 Step 3: Apply the Ostwald dilution expression: ka = molarity * alpha ** 2 / max(1 - alpha, 0.001) = 250000000.0 Final result: 250000000.0

concepts.title: Faraday's First Law: Mass Deposited in Electrolysis
concepts.definition: The mass of substance liberated at an electrode is proportional to the charge passed; the proportionality packs in the metal's molar mass and how many electrons its ion needs.
concepts.key_idea: Charge is current times seconds; each mole of metal costs n Faradays, so moles deposited equal charge over nF, and one Faraday is about 96500 coulombs.
concepts.textbook_ref: lech102.txt, Section 2.6 Faraday's laws and Example 2.10
question_patterns: calculate the mass of copper deposited when a copper sulfate solution is electrolysed for 10 minutes at 1.5 amperes
find how much nickel plates out at the cathode with a 5 ampere current run for 20 minutes
determine the mass of metal liberated during electrolysis from the current, time and electrode reaction
what mass of silver is deposited by a given charge passed through silver nitrate solution
use Faraday first law to convert ampere seconds into grams of deposited metal
compute the deposit formed at a cathode when a stated current flows for a stated duration

solution_steps.action: Multiply current by time to get the charge
solution_steps.explain: 1.5 A for 600 s delivers 900 C.

solution_steps.action: Convert charge to moles of metal
solution_steps.explain: Copper needs 2 electrons per atom, so 900 over 2 times 96487 gives 0.00466 mol.

solution_steps.action: Convert moles to mass
solution_steps.explain: 0.00466 mol times 63 g per mol leaves about 0.294 g of copper on the cathode.

worked_examples.question: Using Faraday's First Law: Mass Deposited in Electrolysis, compute the result for current_amp = 3, time_sec = 3, n_electrons = 3, faraday_const = 2, molar_mass_metal = 2.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Multiply current by time to get the charge: charge_coulomb = current_amp * time_sec = 9.0 Step 2: Convert charge to moles of metal: moles_metal = charge_coulomb / (n_electrons * faraday_const) = 1.5 Step 3: Convert moles to mass: mass_metal = moles_metal * molar_mass_metal = 3.0 Final result: 3.0

worked_examples.question: Using Faraday's First Law: Mass Deposited in Electrolysis, compute the result for current_amp = 4, time_sec = 4, n_electrons = 4, faraday_const = 3, molar_mass_metal = 3.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Multiply current by time to get the charge: charge_coulomb = current_amp * time_sec = 16.0 Step 2: Convert charge to moles of metal: moles_metal = charge_coulomb / (n_electrons * faraday_const) = 1.333333 Step 3: Convert moles to mass: mass_metal = moles_metal * molar_mass_metal = 4.0 Final result: 4.0

concepts.title: Charge Required for an Electrode Reaction
concepts.definition: The electricity needed to reduce or oxidise a stated amount of substance is fixed by the electron count in the half equation: each mole of change consumes that many Faradays.
concepts.key_idea: One mole of Al3+ to Al swallows 3 Faradays near 289500 C, MnO4 minus to Mn2+ takes 5; dividing the coulomb figure by 96500 restates it in Faradays.
concepts.textbook_ref: lech102.txt, Section 2.6 Faraday's laws, Examples on charge requirement
question_patterns: calculate the charge required to reduce 1 mol of Al3+ ions to aluminium metal
how many coulombs are needed to convert 1 mol of MnO4 minus into Mn2+
find the electricity in coulombs for the oxidation of 1 mol of water to oxygen
determine how much electricity in terms of Faraday produces 20 g of calcium from molten CaCl2
what quantity of electricity reduces a stated number of moles in a given half reaction
compute the charge passed when a stated mass of metal is produced electrolytically from its melt

solution_steps.action: Turn the stated mass into moles of substance
solution_steps.explain: Divide by the molar mass; for a one mole case the ratio is simply 1.

solution_steps.action: Multiply by the electron count and the Faraday
solution_steps.explain: Aluminium takes 3 electrons per ion, so 1 times 3 times 96487 gives about 289461 C; divide by 96500 to read it as 3 Faradays.

worked_examples.question: Using Charge Required for an Electrode Reaction, compute the result for mass_sample = 3, molar_mass_substance = 3, z_electrons = 3, faraday_const = 2.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Turn the stated mass into moles of substance: moles_substance = mass_sample / molar_mass_substance = 1.0 Step 2: Multiply by the electron count and the Faraday: charge_coulomb = moles_substance * z_electrons * faraday_const = 6.0 Final result: 6.0

worked_examples.question: Using Charge Required for an Electrode Reaction, compute the result for mass_sample = 4, molar_mass_substance = 4, z_electrons = 4, faraday_const = 3.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Turn the stated mass into moles of substance: moles_substance = mass_sample / molar_mass_substance = 1.0 Step 2: Multiply by the electron count and the Faraday: charge_coulomb = moles_substance * z_electrons * faraday_const = 12.0 Final result: 12.0

concepts.title: Primary Batteries, Secondary Batteries and Fuel Cells
concepts.definition: Practical galvanic devices come in three kinds: primary cells that die once (dry cell, mercury cell), secondary cells that recharge by reversing the reaction (lead storage, nickel-cadmium), and fuel cells fed continuously with reactants such as hydrogen and oxygen.
concepts.formula: battery class = reuse mode (once, rechargeable, continuous feed)
concepts.key_idea: The lead storage cell reverses Pb plus PbO2 with sulfuric acid on charging; a mercury cell keeps constant voltage because no solution ion changes concentration; the hydrogen oxygen fuel cell reaches about 70 percent efficiency and releases only water.
question_patterns: explain why a mercury cell maintains a steady voltage through its life
state the electrode reactions of the lead storage battery during discharge and recharging
distinguish a primary battery from a secondary battery with one example of each
write the overall reaction of the hydrogen oxygen fuel cell and note its efficiency advantage
identify which battery is recharged by passing current in the opposite direction
describe the construction of the dry cell naming its anode and cathode materials

solution_steps.action: Check whether the cell reaction is reversible or single use
solution_steps.explain: Primary cells like the dry cell cannot be recharged; secondary cells like lead storage can.

solution_steps.action: Recall the electrode chemistry of the named cell
solution_steps.explain: Lead battery: Pb and PbO2 plates in sulfuric acid; fuel cell: hydrogen burned electrochemically at porous electrodes.

solution_steps.action: State the reuse mode and key advantage
solution_steps.explain: Rechargeability for secondary cells, steady voltage for mercury cells, continuous clean output for fuel cells.

concepts.title: Corrosion as an Electrochemical Process
concepts.definition: Rusting and similar surface decay behave like short-circuited galvanic cells on the metal: one spot oxidises iron while another reduces oxygen, and the ferrous ions finally leave as hydrated ferric oxide.
concepts.formula: corrosion cell = anodic spot (metal dissolves) plus cathodic spot (oxygen reduced)
concepts.key_idea: Iron dissolves at the anodic spot (minus 0.44 V couple) while oxygen plus hydrogen ions is reduced at the cathodic spot (plus 1.23 V); painting, plating or a sacrificial magnesium or zinc electrode blocks the damage.
question_patterns: explain how rusting of iron sets up an electrochemical cell on its surface
identify the anode and cathode reactions during the corrosion of iron in moist air
state why sacrificial electrodes of magnesium or zinc protect an iron object
describe the electrochemical mechanism behind tarnishing of silver or green coating on copper
what are the half reactions that turn iron into hydrated ferric oxide rust
list methods of preventing corrosion and the principle each one uses

solution_steps.action: Point out the anodic spot where the metal oxidises
solution_steps.explain: Fe goes to Fe2 plus releasing electrons that travel through the metal.

solution_steps.action: Point out the cathodic spot where oxygen is reduced
solution_steps.explain: Oxygen with hydrogen ions takes up those electrons to form water.

solution_steps.action: Follow the secondary oxidation to the rust and the prevention logic
solution_steps.explain: Ferrous ions oxidise further to ferric oxide hydrate; cutting air or water contact, or adding a more reactive sacrificial metal, stops the cycle.

worked_examples.question: The cell reaction Mg(s) + 2 Ag+(0.0001 M) gives Mg2+(0.130 M) + 2 Ag(s) has a standard emf of 3.17 V. What is its emf at these concentrations?
worked_examples.solution: Q = 0.130 times 0.0001 squared; log Q near minus 7.11. Nernst correction: 0.059 over 2 times minus 7.11 = minus 0.21 V.

worked_examples.question: For Cu(s) + 2 Ag+(aq) the standard emf is 0.46 V. Find Kc at 298 K.
worked_examples.solution: log Kc = 2 times 0.46 over 0.059 = 15.6.
worked_examples.answer: Kc near 3.92 times ten to the 15

worked_examples.question: The conductivity of 0.20 M KCl at 298 K is 0.0248 S per cm. Find its molar conductivity.
worked_examples.solution: Lambda m = 1000 times kappa over c = 1000 times 0.0248 over 0.20.

worked_examples.question: Copper sulfate is electrolysed 10 minutes at 1.5 A. What mass of copper plates out?
worked_examples.solution: Q = 900 C; moles Cu = 900 over (2 times 96487) = 0.00466; mass = 0.00466 times 63.
